articles.title: AI Can Never Give Lawyers All Their Time Back
articles.content:
8am spent its Kaleidoscope conference in Las Vegas last week promising lawyers their time back. CEO Jeff Hughes opened with the company’s “Admin Misery Index” — 1,600 lawyers surveyed, 73 percent calling busywork a substantial problem, “at least 200 hours per year” lost to it — and nearly everything after that was about returning those hours. Since it’s 2026, you know the answer to getting that time back is in AI.
With a couple weeks to reflect on this message, what stands out most is all the time AI can never give back.
My personal experience with the conference underscored the problem. I arrived in Vegas — an ironic choice to place the 8am conference in a town where time has no meaning — having spent twenty-some consecutive hours awake. Over the next two nights, I managed to contract a nasty-yet-thankfully-short-lived spot of food poisoning that left me up most of that night, and the next night I left the closing party for a 12:30 a.m. red-eye. Most of that was self-inflicted, but none of it was delegable to AI.
It’s a well-worn cliche that agents can’t go to court for you, but that’s really the tip of the iceberg for what they can’t do. Perhaps it’s better to think of AI as maximizing what you do with your non-delegable time. C. Northcote Parkinson wrote a 1955 piece in the Economist arguing that work expands to fill the time available. So far that seems to be the fate of the AI economy.
It was an earlier report by 8am itself that showed lawyers billing more time per matter than before even as AI use skyrocketed. While AI skeptics will blame this on nervous lawyers burning more time to check against hallucinations than they would’ve doing the research themselves — and caution may contribute some — the overwhelming contributor seems to be a combination of AI uncovering rabbit holes that lawyers wouldn’t have thought of otherwise, and — more relevant to 8am — lawyers having time in their pockets to do lawyering that used to be tied up in practice management tasks.
Moving tasks to the delegable column just moves time to the non-delegable tasks that used to get short-changed.
While at the conference, I moderated a panel titled “Expanding Into New Practice Areas,” with Krystal Champlin-Gerage of RJH Consulting and Tristian Shannon of the Law Offices of Giselle Rodriguez. The topic, mixing business strategy and marketing, was intended as helpful content to the small and solo audience as opposed to a pitch for the 8am product. The fix for a firm looking to expand is partly technical. Champlin-Gerage encouraged lawyers to mine their own data to see where clients keep asking for help that the lawyers don’t yet offer, which certainly requires software tracking unless you have Bob Cratchit working holidays to compile all your billing nuances by hand. However, the rest of the journey is more about people than software, as expanding firms need to build out a strong network of mentors willing to lend expertise as lawyers develop their new practice competence. “I have a mentor for everything,” Shannon said.
But the unspoken reality looming over the whole conversation is that nobody can do all the work of identifying a business opportunity, spinning up the necessary competence, and getting off the ground if they don’t have the time to commit. If administrative tasks eat up half the day, that’s half a day of business development lost. A lawyer isn’t getting time back. The time just moves to a new task that would never get accomplished without the time to build human relationships that AI can’t manage.
Niki Black of 8am — a columnist here at Above the Law — moderated a panel called “The Attorney’s Guide to AI,” that proved exactly how scattered the profession’s experience with AI is in 2026. The panel, including Jared Correia of Red Cave Legal, solo practitioner Bradley Clark, and Smith.ai CEO Suresh Khanna, set out to help lawyers elevate their AI chops. Clark described his approach to skills and agents, automating his practice and building out tools to get deeper insights on his motions before he files them, some of the audience were just looking for someone to tell them who this Claude guy is that everyone keeps talking about.
The panel pivoted on the fly, backtracking to the basics: pick Claude or ChatGPT, talk to them in plain English, etc. That’s the echo chamber we fall into hopscotching the country to these legal tech conferences. Vibes tell us that lawyers are beyond ChatGPT and ready to build out their agentic intake process, while in reality most lawyers are still a little confused by Clippy.
When I talked to Hughes later, he suggested that we’re still in an era where conferences should build AI training content around tracks, with material explicitly labeled for beginners and for the advanced. A great idea, but another reminder that the distance between “which website” and “orchestrating sub-agents” isn’t getting closed by labs releasing bigger models, but by humans putting in the hours. Non-delegable, human hours that they can only spare when something else is taken off their plate.
We put on a live edition of Legaltech Week at the show, breaking down the key takeaways. As usual, I provided my less-than-shiny view of agentic AI. It’s the great hope of the AI crowd, who desperately need users to build token infernos if they ever hope to monetize the technology into even a breakeven proposition, but for lawyers the supposed safety valve for a swarm of sub-agents is an empty promise. A partner who’s going to sit down at the end and read 300 pages of agent audit logs? Let’s be real. I’ve said it before, but “I’ll keep you in the loop” is something you say before blowing someone off — you should read “human in the loop” the same way.
This is the problem with framing AI as a time saver alone. The misanthropic investors behind this technology want it to replace human work altogether so they can finally snuff out humanity and see if Optimus Prime rises in its place, but the reality is that a lot of this work is still going to be human. The trick is moving the work that can be automated off of the lawyers so they can make the most of the work that can’t be.
And understanding that there will be time that can never be shunted off to a bot — at least not without a radical shift in the underlying technology — changes how you think about AI. It ceases to have the snake oil quality of promising a future 2-hour work week, and becomes the technology that gives lawyers permission to get deeper on their matters or push into new fields.
For a conference all about time, it’s worth remembering what the 8am name change was all about. Lawyers trying to stay ahead of their administrative misery tend to do that work before 8:00 a.m. and the company’s name promises to supercharge that pre-8 a.m. work. But lawyers aren’t the type of people who will take their newfound 7-8 a.m. freedom to lounge around. They’re going to fill it with the human-only tasks that they always meant to do, but never had the time.
And, yes, occasionally to take advantage of the non-delegable job of recovering from all-night nausea.
8am covered my travel and lodging to attend Kaleidoscope.

articles.title: Law School In The Age Of AI: Rethinking It From The Ground Up
articles.content:
We have all heard it. AI is creating a generation of mindless lawyers who won’t know how to think. They won’t know how to write. They won’t know how to do research. They’ll just type a question into AI, copy whatever they get back and merrily send slop on its way.
And with AI, law firms will no longer have the tasks for young lawyers to do, through which they learn how to practice. Clients won’t pay for that anymore. So we either find another way to train young lawyers, or we wait for the day when those lawyers run the profession. Like robots. Producing not only AI slop but AI slop advice.
Traditional Law School Thinking
If we opt for the former, it shifts the focus to the law schools to take on this training role. Ahh, the law schools. You know the ones. They teach by the Socratic method. Casebooks. Core courses. One five-hour exam at the end of the year. They spend enormous amounts of time teaching students to “think like a lawyer” and precious little time teaching them how to be a lawyer. When you think of law schools, think Professor Kingsfield from the 1973 movie “The Paper Chase.” Yes, 1973. That’s kind of the point: most law schools are doing things as they have always done them. Some are even banning the use of technology and AI. That’s like driving at 120 miles per hour and trying to steer while looking in the rearview mirror. Brilliant.
The RelFest Panel
I attended a 45-minute session at RelFest (formerly, Relativity Fest) entitled “Shaping the Next Generation of Legal Professionals.” It was another one of those substantive nonsalesy sessions Relativity excels in, and I was all ears. It was supposed to be a three-person panel plus a moderator. The panelists were listed in the course description as April Dawson, professor of law and faculty director of AI initiative, Howard University; Bobby Williams, director, iDS/NExT; and Dorna Moini, VP, product management, Relativity and founder of Gavel. Relativity’s Adam Rouse moderated.
But when I walked in, to my surprise, none other than Dan Linna, director of law and technology initiatives at Northwestern Pritzker School of Law, was also on the podium. I’ve known Dan for a long time. Once upon a time, he helped me try to develop a new way to handle complex cases by using ALSPs to do most of the work. And having the partner concentrate on and get paid for things only the partner could provide: judgment and experience.
It never got off the ground. Too many sacred cows. Too much change. But Dan was all in. He likes challenging norms. He was and is one of the leading thinkers in legal. When I saw him on the panel, I knew it was going to be a mind-bending session.
Law School Mavericks
And it was. Because this panel was not all about doom and gloom for law schools’ role in training young lawyers. They weren’t sitting around lamenting how AI was going to destroy legal education. Or detecting if students were secretly using AI.
Nay, nay, nay. This panel was all about the opportunities that AI holds for real training and producing graduates who are not like today’s first-year associates. Who are instead more like third- or fourth-year ones. And make no mistake, these panelists were all about rethinking law school from the ground up, not just tinkering with yesterday’s curriculum.
Consider what Linna is doing. He has created an AI Socratic tutor students use most every day. So instead of getting called on a couple of times a semester, you’re on the hot seat constantly. He’s also created coaches that give feedback on the work the students have done. He requires students to give in-class presentations.
He’s created an oral argument simulator and a simulation that forces a student to go through the steps to prepare for trial. And the beauty of all these tools is rather than the associate trying to grab feedback from a partner catch-as-catch-can, they can be used over and over. Believe me, I know how the other way goes. Partner stressed for time. Associate stressed for time. In bad moods. Both know the client likely won’t pay for time spent in training; got to keep those billable quotas in mind, you know. Neither fully invested. Linna, on the other hand, even takes time at the end of the course to meet with each student to ask them about what they have learned and the papers they have authored.
Dawson came at it another way. One of the classes she teaches is admin law. Not the sexiest course in law school, I know. But Dawson teaches it with what she calls a “tech focus.” She requires her students to use AI tools to accelerate their learning, not detract from it. She gives the students a reading assignment and then asks them to complete the reading using AI as a companion. She explained that when she was in law school, she might have to read an assignment, a case, or an opinion several times to understand it. Yep, I remember that all too well: it’s like starting a book in the middle and trying to figure it out.
But with an AI companion, her students can stop and ask the tool questions. What does this term mean? What did the judge mean by this cite and sentence? And so on. But here’s the important part. After reading what’s assigned, the student asks the AI tool to give them a Socratic quiz. The student then supplies Dawson with a link to the completed quiz so she can assess how they did and help them improve.
Another thing Dawson does. She requires her students in her other classes to use the tool for pro se litigants, Courtroom5. She uses AI to create a pro se persona. She then asks the student to be that person and use the Courtroom5 tool to see what it’s like for pro se litigants to try to navigate the system. To see what it’s like for the rest of the world.
It’s About Life Skills
The panel was also all over the need for law schools to teach life skills. Like human relations. Like design thinking. Communication. Project management. Williams put it well: “life is project management.” He also uses things like improv to help teach people how to deal with human situations.
All this and more is going on in the heads of these passionate people. They realize that while school is great and AI is great, the more important thing is to teach law students how to deal with the reality of practicing law. As Moini put it, you can prepare all you want in advance for an oral argument. But you don’t really know how well you know something until the judges start firing questions at you. Starting with the one you didn’t think of.
Simulations. Socratic tutors. Coaches. All things designed to give law students and, for that matter, young lawyers, the kind of real-life experiences they need to practice law.
But It’s Not Going To Be Easy
Let’s be clear though. This kind of thinking and doing requires, as Linna put it, a change in how law professors teach and how they assess what their students are learning. More quizzes, less reliance on the single end-of-the-year exam.
And as I listened, I kept thinking: this is really a rethinking of legal education. And that requires work. Requires law schools to rethink how and what they are teaching. It requires the courage to try and fail in the face of others in academia who scoff at change and what they are doing. It requires passion and putting students’ needs first. It’s a lot harder than standing in front of a class and teaching the same way you always have.
It also requires giving up a large piece of hubris. I heard a story once about a legal innovator who took what he thought was a good idea to a law school. The school rejected it, saying, “If it was a good idea, we would have thought of it.” Right.
But if what the RelFest panelists are doing and what others at innovative law schools like Vanderbilt and Suffolk are doing is any indication, we are in good hands. And we could be on the eve of better lawyers sooner, instead of more of the same. The kind of lawyers who drive looking ahead, not always looking in the rearview mirror.
Sorry, Kingsfield.
Stephen Embry is a lawyer, speaker, blogger, and writer. He publishes TechLaw Crossroads, a blog devoted to the examination of the tension between technology, the law, and the practice of law.
The post Law School In The Age Of AI: Rethinking It From The Ground Up appeared first on Above the Law.

articles.title: Do You Also Want Your Money Back?
articles.content:
I want my money back. How about you?
The cost of changing the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the “Gulf of America” has been about 500 grand.
I’d like my share back, please.
The cost of changing the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America”? Perplexity can’t help me.
The cost of restoring the name of Mt. Denali to Mt. McKinley? Also unknown.
Now we’re changing “artificial intelligence” to “superintelligence” in all government documents.
Whatever the costs are, I want my share back.
Donald Trump proposes these name changes simply to attract attention and own the libs. Those are fine choices, I suppose, but does he really get to spend my money to indulge his silly narcissistic needs?
Several times, President Trump has tried to strip press credentials from national media because Trump resents negative reporting. Those efforts at stripping press credentials are doomed to fail. But having the government stagger its way to failure incurs a cost — in Department of Justice time and effort, in judicial time deciding those cases, and the like. It’s all government money.
I don’t want to spend my money on Trump’s useless fits of pique. I want my share of the wasted money back.
Same deal with tariffs that legal scholars know will not be permitted. There’re administrative costs in implementing the tariffs, DOJ and court time in striking down the tariffs, administrative time undoing the tariffs and reimbursing money. It’s all waste. I want my share back.
Trump’s a billionaire, and he’s enriching himself by the day. He can afford the cost of silly little games — especially when my money, not his, pays the price of admission.
I’m out here in the cheap seats.
If Trump wants to fight about the name (and membership on the board) of the Institute of Peace, he can do it. But not on my nickel.
If he wants to fight about the name (and membership on the board) of the Kennedy Center, and the cost of losing performers and shutting down the building, he can do it. But not on my nickel.
If Trump wants to destroy a perfectly good East Wing of the White House and replace it with a fancy ballroom, the ballroom would surely make his life more pleasant. But the expense makes my life less pleasant. Let’s stop.
Triumphal arches for no reason other than glorifying Trump? Five million bucks to change the Arts of War and Arts of Peace sculptures (framing the Arlington Memorial Bridge) from bronze to gold leaf? Running public service announcements about how only Trump can keep the communists out of America? Same deal.
Flying to Mar-a-Lago at government expense, with a government security detail, every month or so? It’s nice for Trump; he likes golf. But he’s rich; and he can afford it; and he’s not even paying, for heaven’s sake. Why are we charging me for his luxuries?
Remodeling the Lincoln Bathroom?
Golden doodads in the Oval Office?
Those silly plaques lining the West Wing Colonnade (with Biden depicted as an auto-pen)?
The helipad?
I realize that being president costs the government money. The president has to travel, and be protected, and all that stuff.
But how about the unnecessary stuff? Shouldn’t the president be treating government money as though it were yours?
Because it is.
I want my share back. Do you?
Mark Herrmann spent 17 years as a partner at a leading international law firm and later oversaw litigation, compliance and employment matters at a large international company. He is the author of The Curmudgeon’s Guide to Practicing Law and Drug and Device Product Liability Litigation Strategy (affiliate links). You can reach him by email at inhouse@abovethelaw.com.
